transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-03
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Recording: (internal)

Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Evelyn (LatticeCare Head of ML), Samir (Infra), Noah (CTO), Priya (Data Scientist)

Summary (auto): week six bench readout, routing tune, action items agreed.

[00:00] Jordan Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check — is this still a 42 minute block, right?
[00:08] Evelyn Ortiz: Yeah that's right, we have till about 15:42 our side.
[00:12] Jordan Park: Great. Agenda: quick recap of baseline numbers, Maya will share tuned run, then open Q&A and next steps.
[00:25] Maya Chen: Cool. I'll start with the baseline comparison vs their current vendor — um, we compared three scenarios: hosted with standard routing, hosted with KV caching enabled, and a quantized runtime on a dedicated slot. The headline, for the 512-token synthesis workload, is median latency improved ~18% and p99 improved about 28% versus IncumbentAI when using routing+cache. Throughput saw a 1.5x uplift in tokens per second under batching.
[00:50] Samir Patel: Sorry, can you clarify tokens per… how are you measuring TPS here? Is that aggregate across 8 GPUs?
[01:00] Maya Chen: Good call — these runs were on a 4-GPU dedicated pool, equivalent to your pilot config. We report tokens/sec per GPU and aggregate. So per GPU we saw ~420 tokens/s baseline to ~610 tokens/s after batching and kernel optimizations. Aggregate to about 2.4k tokens/sec. Note that these are lab conditions — network E2E will add latency.
[01:25] Priya Rao: Are the numbers for streaming responses or full completion?
[01:28] Maya Chen: Streaming responses, yes — it's the token emission rate. There's some small variance for long tail prompts.
[01:35] Evelyn Ortiz: The p99 number is what worries me, sometimes our customers hit the tail and it spikes. How did you get 28% improvement there?
[01:42] Maya Chen: We tuned routing to favor low-latency nodes for synchronous calls, kept a small parallel queue for longer contexts, and enabled prefix KV cache which reduces recurrent attention compute for similar prompts. Also we adjusted quantization profile to int8 dynamic which saved time without large quality drop. Caveat: with smaller batch sizes the p99 uplift is less dramatic.
[02:15] Noah Li: Jordan, quick question — when you say quantized, do you mean 4-bit or 8-bit? We tried 4-bit with FastServe and saw hallucinations creep in.
[02:23] Jordan Park: For this run we used int8 dynamic quantization. Maya, feel free to add.
[02:28] Maya Chen: Right, int8 dynamic. 4-bit was explored but not the default for this workload because of QC risk. We can do a sr-run on a small prompt set to validate 4-bit for your domain, but initial eval shows noise on entity consistency.
[02:45] Samir Patel: Network — how much does VPC peering add? The egress numbers from your cloud provider earlier looked high.
[02:53] Maya Chen: Egress depends on topology. For our hosted mode with VPC peering, egress is only inter-region charges; if you use Redwood Private inside your VPC on-prem, egress is internal. Our estimate for your pilot VPC peer was roughly $0.01–$0.02 per 1k tokens egress-equivalent in our projection but that's approximate. We will share raw cost calc in the sheet.
[03:20] Evelyn Ortiz: We need SOC2-level audit logs for every request — can you capture application user ID and trace ID on the audit trail?
[03:27] Jordan Park: Yes, we can surface request-level logs and integrate with your SIEM; we have example exports for Kinesis, Splunk, and S3. We'll send the SOC2 artifacts.
[03:35] Priya Rao: Sorry, small transcription hiccup — when you said "K-V cash" did you mean KV cache?
[03:40] Maya Chen: Ha yes, sorry the auto transcript is funny — KV cache, not cash.
[03:45] Jordan Park: Back to the data: I pulled the lab's p50/p95/p99 table into the shared sheet. For the worst-case prompt bucket we saw p99 drop from 1.8s to 1.3s.
[04:00] Evelyn Ortiz: Is that end-to-end? We need browser-to-response numbers, not just inference.
[04:06] Maya Chen: These are inference-only numbers. We added a 60–120ms simulated network overlay for a separate E2E run; that pushed p99 to ~1.45s. We'll upload both raw traces.
[04:25] Samir Patel: Regarding the baseline, the incumbent (IncumbentAI) uses more aggressive batching which gives better throughput but hurts tail. Can you show a scenario where you match their throughput but improve tail?
[04:38] Maya Chen: Yes — we ran an aggressive batching scenario and matched throughput but p99 widened. The sweet spot in our tests was medium batch with adaptive batching: increase batching in low-load windows and route synchronous calls to low-latency slots. That got near-incumbent throughput while keeping p99 materially better.
[04:58] Priya Rao: You mentioned routing — is that a static policy or ML-based?
[05:02] Maya Chen: Policy-based with heuristics today (latency-first, cost-fallback). We're piloting an adaptive controller that uses recent p99 signals to shift routing, but not in production for this POC.
[05:15] Noah Li: On SLA — what's the guarantee if we move to Dedicated? We need clarity on throughput SLO and scheduled maintenance windows.
[05:23] Jordan Park: Dedicated comes with an SLA; we can map throughput SLOs as part of a reserved capacity contract. I'll attach the draft SLA language.
[05:30] Evelyn Ortiz: Also, for compliance we need KMS integration. Can Redwood use our HSM?
[05:36] Maya Chen: We support customer-managed keys via standard KMS/HSM integrations. We'll include the KMS integration note in the security pack.
[05:45] Samir Patel: Can you walk us through the raw logs format? We need trace ID, token timestamps, and model version.
[05:52] Jordan Park: Yep. We'll include a sample JSON event with trace_id, request_id, model, slot_id, tokens_emitted, and timestamps at token-chunk granularity.
[06:05] Maya Chen: Quick demo slide — here's the left column: baseline, right: tuned. (brief pause) For the tuned run we also turned on prefix caching for sessioned chats; that yielded a 20–25% compute reduction for repeated prompts.
[06:30] Priya Rao: Any quality regression with prefix caching?
[06:33] Maya Chen: Minimal. We ran evals against your validation set — Rouge/F1 unchanged within noise. We did see some small increase in repetition for extremely short prompts — we can tweak cache TTL.
[06:50] Evelyn Ortiz: How does Redwood handle model fallback if a preferred model is down? Our compliance team wants deterministic behavior.
[06:58] Jordan Park: We support fallback chains: explicit model variants with compatibility constraints. You can pin to a model and then have read-only fallback to a quantized variant if capacity drops. All fallbacks are logged for audit.
[07:15] Samir Patel: Logistics — Noah asked for an on-prem smoke test. What does that look like?
[07:21] Maya Chen: Smoke test is a 2-hour run where we deploy a minimal private control plane in your lab, run a subset of the workload with synthetic traffic, collect traces, and validate latency and correctness. Typical checklist: connectivity, KMS handshake, model loading, routing policy verification, and throughput hang tests.
[07:41] Noah Li: We'll need a checklist so my ops team can stand this up.
[07:44] Jordan Park: We'll send a runbook and a Docker/helm quickstart.
[07:48] Priya Rao: Quick tangent — how did FastServe compare?
[07:52] Maya Chen: FastServe did well on bulk throughput but struggled with prefix cache and routing primitives; their p99 was worse in mixed workloads. IncumbentAI is optimized differently — they batch aggressively and sometimes sacrifice tail.
[08:10] Evelyn Ortiz: On the quality front, we saw a few examples where int8 slightly changed entity spelling. Is that reproducible?
[08:18] Maya Chen: In some edge cases yes; that's why we recommend running a domain-specific eval. For your dataset we saw 2% delta on NER metrics at int8 vs FP16, but again depends on prompt style.
[08:35] Jordan Park: Action items recap: we'll upload raw traces and the benchmark CSV; Maya will draft routing policies and suggested quantization profiles; Samir will validate VPC numbers; Evelyn will run another eval pass.
[08:50] Maya Chen: One thing we want to try for week 7 — a short dedicated slot reservation to exercise traffic shaping. If you agree we can reserve a slot for 48 hours next week.
[08:59] Noah Li: We can greenlight a 48-hour slot pending Samir's cost check.
[09:05] Samir Patel: I'll do the cost check but I need the exact egress bytes estimate.
[09:09] Jordan Park: We'll provide that in the sheet.
[09:12] Priya Rao: Any other blockers?
[09:15] Evelyn Ortiz: Security — please send SOC2 and SAML/SSO integration docs.
[09:20] Jordan Park: On it. We'll also include RBAC examples.
[09:24] Maya Chen: One more note — for the routing policy we recommend two live groups: low-latency slots with reserved capacity for sync calls and a cost-tier group for async batches. The controller can fail over between them if latency thresholds are breached.
[09:45] Samir Patel: For the logs, can you include a delta of token timestamps so we can compute serialization overhead?
[09:52] Maya Chen: Yes we'll add token-level deltas.
[10:00] Jordan Park: Ok let's go into the shared sheet and I'll point out the rows. (screen share noise)
[10:12] Maya Chen: Row 12 is the worst-case prompt bucket with p99 numbers. Row 18 shows the aggressive batching run. Row 22 is the quantized int8 run.
[10:30] Priya Rao: I see an anomaly in row 18 — there's a spike at t=00:23 that looks like a GC pause?
[10:36] Maya Chen: That's correct — one of the worker nodes had a background maintenance task during that run. We've annotated that as noisy.
[10:44] Evelyn Ortiz: For the final deliverable — please include both per-request traces and aggregated p99 computations; our compliance team will re-run the math.
[10:52] Jordan Park: We'll provide raw traces and the aggregated sheet and include a small narrative explaining methodology.
[11:00] Noah Li: Timeline-wise, once we get the raw logs and the routing policy, we plan to run a 48-hour fight in week 7 and then decide on reserved capacity. Does that sound right?
[11:10] Jordan Park: Yep. We'll aim to have everything in place by 2026-11-06 so you can kick off the 48-hour run on 2026-11-09 or 11-10 depending on ops availability.
[11:22] Samir Patel: I'll try for 11-09 but will confirm.
[11:26] Evelyn Ortiz: Any final questions?
[11:30] Priya Rao: None from data.
[11:32] Maya Chen: Quick check — do you want us to include a small synthetic load generator repo so you can run locally?
[11:36] Noah Li: Yes that would help.
[11:38] Jordan Park: Great. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with attachments and the action items.
[11:43] Evelyn Ortiz: Thanks all.

End of transcript.
